items.title: Over the summer, we have been sprinting on safety priorities; it's more important than ever for capa...
items.content:
Over the summer, we have been sprinting on safety priorities; it's more important than ever for capabilities and safeguards to advance together. We have more to do but have made a lot of progress. We are also going to be launching our next model soon.

There is an obvious tension here: on one hand, Astra is very good and we are excited to see what people will build with it. We are proud of our work.

On the other hand, we are clearly in a phase of development where we believe caution is warranted, and we are pacing our progress to ensure that we can meet the safety standards required by new capability levels.

Astra has been done training for a while now and is a significant step forward in both capabilities and alignment. For the models after that, we have been slowing things as needed to ensure that we can do sufficient work on safety and alignment.

AI is getting extremely capable; no one fully understands the consequences of this. Managing the transition to a world with abundant and powerful AI to optimize for safety and benefits to people should be one of the highest priorities in the world. It is our highest priority at OpenAI.

We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us. We know it is much more discordant for other people. And yet, we believe strongly that the world needs to understand where AI is going and how models perform in the real world. More importantly, we believe the world will need aligned AI to manage the future phases of this transition.

An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.

So we hope you enjoy our new model, and we hope the world continues to take what’s happening in AI extremely seriously.

Test-time scaling has two axes: running agents over longer timeframes (depth), and running a larger number of agents (breadth).

Everybody knows about the first axis, but the second one is just as important when solving hard problems that require broad search.

items.title: Remember that every news announcement from an AI lab is about $20,000 in product and marketing insig...
items.content:
Remember that every news announcement from an AI lab is about $20,000 in product and marketing insights for free. 

When they provide a few bullets of what a new model can do, it’s based off of the previous complaints and usage patterns of millions of customers. 

And we also need to remember that, in my opinion, Claude Code is in second place behind Codex right now. 

Read between the lines. 

This announcement tells me the following ⬇️ 

- Claude Code was annoying people by giving up early or jumping the gun on muddy assignments. I’ve seen Codex “give up” less, so that’s also competitive positioning. 
- Spreadsheets are a big enough use case that they get their own bullet! Excel and Google Sheets still likely hold the lion’s share…probably more Excel than GSheets if we look across all businesses in the US
- 5.1 positioning (rather than .2 or .5) possibly to not oversell capabilities or spook the market 
- We’re still in a compute-constrained world (Fable 5.1 can be used for 50% of Max plan but need to see whether that’s on an hourly or weekly basis) 
- Verification is still a big ask from business users (I can confirm that this is one of the top 3 questions I get asked by business professionals)

Three ways you get in trouble when building an app:

1. Always calling the best model
2. Always calling the cheapest model
3. Always calling a mid model

The first strategy will be very expensive. The second strategy is just dumb. The third strategy is just mediocre.

The proper solution is to use a router and decide which model is best for a particular request.

Check out these guys. Their platform lets you select a model and a specific reasoning effort for each request.

This keeps the quality of the best models while costing much, much less.

But if my house was on fire, and I called the fire department and told them my house was “breathing smoke”, and they warned me not to use humanizing language, my damn house is still on fire and I need the fire put out. 

(Bad analogy but you get it. A fight against the language is not a fight against the key concept and takeaway.) 

Other than the anthropomorphic language, what other pushback do people have?

items.content: Autoresearch is great when you can throw "stuff at the wall" (i.e. run many fast experiments). What if experiments take weeks or months to run and millions of dollars instead? - no real willingness to solve problems
- nor an acceptance of people offering to solve their problems (out of pride)
- simply too much regulation so the problem cannot be solved without a license or long approval time
- very low standards of what is deemed acceptable so the problem isn't seen as a problem in the first place

The rest of the world really mostly functions like this (except Asia and a few countries in the Middle East)

items.title: You are happy with the benefits digital transformation brings to your company, but now you are disco...
items.content:
You are happy with the benefits digital transformation brings to your company, but now you are discovering a “hidden tax”: digital friction.

It appears when people repeat work, switch between systems, or wait for information, consuming time and capacity. 

Microblog @antgrasso 

Let me explain digital friction “papele papele,” as we say in Naples: plain and simple.

An employee updates a customer record in the CRM, then copies the same information into another system because the two platforms do not communicate.

Five minutes disappear. Multiply that by hundreds of people every day and the cost is no longer small.

Or take an approval process. The request is already inside a digital workflow, but someone still exports a file and sends it by email for another check.

The technology is there.
The work is still moving twice.

Digital friction often hides in repeated work or waiting between systems.

The answer is not another transformation project. Start by watching how work actually moves and identify where people repeat actions or leave one system just to complete a task in another.

Then remove the friction that adds no judgment.

A process can be digital and still waste time.
That waste is the “hidden tax” you keep paying until someone looks closely enough to see it.
